scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In ancient Sparta, children began learning the Pyrrhichios at age five, turning simulated spear thrusts and dodges into a rigid martial education.
This is Pyrrhichios. Antiquity.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Pyrrhichios originated in ancient Greece, likely of Dorian origin, with roots tracing back to Minoan Crete.
Historical references identify figures like Thaletas of Crete as a musical arranger for these dances in Sparta.
It was performed widely across the Greek world from the Black Sea to Cyprus, evolving from practical battle preparation into a staple of civic festivals, athletic games, and symposia.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance was deeply tied to religious cults honoring Zeus, Cybèle, Artemis, Athena, and the Dioscuri.

It served a dual purpose: practical martial training to increase warrior agility before battle, and ritual performance during funerals, civic games, and diplomatic banquets to celebrate unity or victory.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers wore full hoplite armor, carrying shields, spears, and helmets.
The choreography involved quick movements simulating the avoidance of blows and darts, attacking enemies, advancing, retreating, dropping to the ground as if wounded, and springing back up.
It was performed as a solo, in dueling pairs facing each other, or in large circular groups by men, youths, boys, and occasionally women.
Watch for hoplite combat simulation.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance was exclusively accompanied by the sound of the aulos, a double-reed ancient Greek wind instrument.
The musical time was quick and light, corresponding directly to the metric foot known as the pyrrhic.
Listen for the aulos.
Played to the shrill sound of the aulos, featuring a quick and light tempo characteristic of the pyrrhic metric foot, driving rapid physical simulations of combat.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wore complete military armor including helmets, greaves, shields, and tunics—often traditionally associated with the vermilion red color of blood.
Settings ranged from Spartan training grounds and the Athenian palaestra to festive banquets (symposia) and grand ritual spaces during the Panathenaic Games and Gymnopédies.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Achilles is mythically credited by Aristotle with creating the dance around Patroclus's funeral pyre.
Xenophon documented its performance at a banquet in Kotyora, and Plato detailed its tactical mechanics in his work Leges.
Regional expressions varied from the strict martial training drills of Sparta to the competitive displays of Athenian youth in the Panathenaic Games.

The dance shares a lineage with other ancient Greek armed dances and ritual traditions such as the dances of the Korybantes and Curetes, influencing later historical conceptions of European weapon dances.
